deep.reconstruction: Section 2 of E477 applies the general identity of Section 1 to power sums. Section 1 says that if Σa_k = t, Σα_k = u and Σa_kα_k = v (each with first term 1), then Σ_k a_k(Σ_{j≤k} α_j) + Σ_k α_k(Σ_{j≤k} a_j) = tu + v. Euler now takes a_k = k^{-m} and α_k = k^{-n}. He writes ∫1/z^m for the sum Σ_{k≥1} k^{-m}, so ∫1/z^m = ζ(m). He then forms two series. P = Σ_{k≥1} k^{-m} Σ_{j=1}^{k} j^{-n}, which is the non-strict ('star') double zeta value ζ*(m,n). Q = Σ_{k≥1} k^{-n} Σ_{j=1}^{k} j^{-m} = ζ*(n,m). The principle of §1 gives P + Q = ζ(m)ζ(n) + ζ(m+n). In strict form this is ζ(m,n) + ζ(n,m) = ζ(m)ζ(n) − ζ(m+n), the simplest stuffle (harmonic-product) relation. Euler draws the consequence: if either double series were known, the other would follow. He takes ζ(m) as known, since for even m he had evaluated it via π, and the next page adds that for odd m good numerical approximations are easy to obtain. The purpose is to reduce the 'singular series' (double harmonic-type sums suggested by Goldbach) to single zeta values. The next page sets m = n and gets ζ*(n,n) = ½ζ(n)² + ½ζ(2n).
errors: No genuine error. P and Q converge only when the outer exponent exceeds 1, and ζ(m), ζ(n) need m, n > 1. On the following page Euler applies the m = n = 1 case formally with the divergent Δ = Σ1/k. That case is meaningful only as a statement about divergent quantities or partial sums, not about convergent series.

ideas.what: Symmetric (reflection) relation ζ*(m,n) + ζ*(n,m) = ζ(m)ζ(n) + ζ(m+n), obtained by multiplying two series and splitting the double sum along the diagonal.
ideas.modern_name: Stuffle / harmonic product relation for double zeta values (depth-2 sum formula precursor)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E477, with Goldbach correspondence 1742–43); modern theory by Hoffman, Zagier and others (1990s)
ideas.where_published: E477, Novi Comm. Acad. Sci. Petrop. 20 (1776); Euler–Goldbach letters of 1742

ideas.what: Notation ∫1/z^m for the full sum Σ k^{-m}, used as the 'known' building block (even values via π).

deep.surprise_reason: This is the well-known opening of Euler's double zeta paper. The stuffle reflection relation is universally credited to Euler and Goldbach in the multiple zeta value literature.
